owasp.title: Broken Access Control
owasp.summary: Users can act outside their permissions: reaching another tenant's records, calling an admin route, or changing an id in a URL and getting away with it.

owasp.title: Cryptographic Failures
owasp.summary: Sensitive data is transmitted or stored without adequate protection: plaintext transport, weak or homemade algorithms, or keys handled as ordinary strings.

owasp.title: Injection
owasp.summary: Untrusted input reaches an interpreter as code: SQL, shell, template, or the DOM. The classic and still one of the most damaging classes.

owasp.title: Insecure Design
owasp.summary: The flaw is in what was built, not in how it was coded: a missing rate limit, a recovery flow that trusts an email address, a threat never considered.

owasp.title: Security Misconfiguration
owasp.summary: The software is fine; the way it is set up is not. Default credentials, verbose errors, permissive CORS, missing headers, debug features left enabled.

owasp.title: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
owasp.summary: A dependency has a known vulnerability, or is too old to be receiving fixes.

owasp.title: Identification and Authentication Failures
owasp.summary: Identity can be assumed rather than proven: credentials in source, sessions that never expire, tokens signed with a guessable key.

owasp.title: Software and Data Integrity Failures
owasp.summary: Code or data is trusted without verifying where it came from: unsigned updates, unpinned CI actions, deserialisation of attacker-controlled payloads.

owasp.title: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
owasp.summary: An attack leaves no trace, or the trace itself leaks: unlogged auth failures, and secrets written into logs.

owasp.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
owasp.summary: The server fetches a URL the user chose, and can be pointed at internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or the loopback interface.

asi.title: Agent Goal Hijack
asi.summary: The agent is redirected to pursue an attacker's objective — through instruction text it reads as authoritative, or content it treats as data and then obeys.

asi.title: Tool Misuse and Exploitation
asi.summary: A tool the agent legitimately holds is used for something it was not scoped for, or is fed arguments that turn it into a different capability.

asi.title: Agent Identity and Privilege Abuse
asi.summary: The agent acts with more authority than the task needs: credentials in reach of repository-controlled commands, pre-approved permissions, redirected traffic.

asi.title: Agentic Supply Chain Compromise
asi.summary: Code, tools, or instructions reach the agent from a source nobody vetted: a run-time package resolve, an unpinned MCP server, a third-party marketplace.

asi.title: Unexpected Code Execution
asi.summary: Opening a repository, or letting the agent take one step in it, runs code the developer never asked to run.

asi.title: Memory and Context Poisoning
asi.summary: Durable state the agent carries between turns or sessions is written by an attacker and read back as trusted context.

asi.title: Insufficient Human Oversight
asi.summary: The approval step that was supposed to bound the blast radius is absent, pre-answered, or worded so it is always accepted.

asi.title: Multi-Agent and Orchestration Exploitation
asi.summary: One agent's output becomes another's instruction, and a boundary that existed on paper does not exist in the message flow.

asi.title: Insufficient Agent Observability
asi.summary: What the agent did cannot be reconstructed afterwards: no record of the tool calls, the inputs, or the decision that authorised them.

asi.title: Unbounded Autonomy
asi.summary: The agent is permitted to act without a ceiling on scope, spend, or duration, so a single wrong step is not a bounded mistake.
